title: Your money page — what it shows

steps.path: The top of a new page in your Pages list
steps.headline: What big number should sit at the top of the page?
steps.today: There is no money page. To see where you stand you open Capital One, Amex, Robinhood, Wells Fargo and the loan sites one at a time.
steps.problem: Every account tells you one slice. Nothing adds them up, so the question "am I okay right now?" needs mental math across six apps.
steps.proposal: One large number at the top, with smaller totals under it. Pick which number earns the top spot.

options.label: Net worth
options.summary: Everything you have (cash, savings, investments) minus everything you owe (cards, loans).
pros: The single truest "where do I stand" number.
Goes up as loans shrink, so paying debt feels like progress.
cons: Can be negative for years with student loans, which can feel discouraging.
Swings with the stock market even when nothing else changed.

options.label: Cash available
options.summary: Checking plus savings, minus what is due on cards this month.
pros: Answers "can I afford this right now?"
Ignores long-term loans and stock swings.
cons: Hides the size of your loans entirely.

options.label: Total owed
options.summary: Every card, loan and Affirm plan added together.
pros: Keeps debt payoff front and center.
cons: Says nothing about what you have.

steps.path: The list of accounts under the big number
steps.headline: Should accounts be grouped by kind, or by bank?
steps.today: Each bank's own app shows only that bank, mixing its checking and its card on one screen.
steps.problem: Your cards are spread over four companies and your loans over three, so a bank-by-bank list never shows "all my cards" in one place.
steps.proposal: The page groups accounts one way, with a subtotal for each group.

options.label: By kind
options.summary: Checking, Savings, Investments, Credit cards, Loans, Bills — each with a subtotal.
pros: "How much do I owe on cards?" is one subtotal.
Matches the question you usually ask.
cons: Capital One shows up in two groups (checking and card).

options.label: By bank
pros: Mirrors how you log in, so you know where to go to fix something.
cons: Totals by kind need mental math again.

steps.path: Each credit card in the Credit cards group
steps.headline: How should each card show how close you are to its limit?
steps.today: Each card's app shows a balance and a limit as two separate numbers.
steps.problem: You want to see how close you are to your limits across five cards at a glance, without dividing in your head.
steps.proposal: Each card gets a bar that fills as the balance grows. The bar changes color past a warning point. Pick the warning point.

options.label: Warn at 30%
options.summary: The bar turns amber past 30% of the limit, red past 80%.
pros: 30% is the commonly cited point where credit scores start to dip, so it warns before it costs you.
cons: May look "amber" often, which can feel naggy.

options.label: Warn at 80%
options.summary: The bar only changes color near the limit.
pros: Calm most of the time; only shouts when it matters for declined purchases.
cons: Gives no early hint about your credit score.

options.label: Numbers only
options.summary: Balance and limit as text, no bar.
pros: Compact.
cons: Back to dividing in your head.

steps.path: A Bills section on the page
steps.headline: Should the page list upcoming payments by due date?
steps.today: Your car payment, Liberty Mutual, Visible, loan payments, card minimums and Affirm plans are each due on their own date, tracked in their own apps or emails.
steps.problem: Nothing shows "what is due this week" across all of them, so a due date can slip by.
steps.proposal: A Bills list sorted by the next due date, showing amount and how many days are left.

options.label: List by due date
pros: See the next two weeks of payments at once.
Card and loan due dates can fill in automatically from the bank where available.
cons: Bills from Liberty Mutual and Visible must be entered by you or by me, since they can't connect.

options.label: Monthly total only
pros: One number: what leaves your accounts each month.
cons: Doesn't warn you about a specific upcoming date.

options.label: No bills
pros: Simpler page; balances only.
cons: Misses half of what you described wanting.

steps.path: An Income line on the page
steps.headline: Should the page show your regular income next to your bills?
steps.today: Paychecks land in checking with nothing labeling them as income.
steps.problem: Without income on the page, you can't see "money in vs. money out" for the month.
steps.proposal: You (or I) enter each regular income source once — amount and how often — and the page shows monthly income beside monthly bills.

options.label: Show income
pros: See whether bills fit inside income at a glance.
cons: One more thing to keep current when pay changes.

options.label: Leave for later
pros: Smaller first version.
cons: No money-in vs money-out view yet.

steps.path: A chart under the big number
steps.headline: Should the page remember past totals and draw a chart over time?
steps.today: Banks show today's balance. Seeing how your overall picture changed needs months of statements.
steps.problem: Without history you can't tell if you are getting ahead or falling behind.
steps.proposal: Each day the page refreshes, it keeps that day's totals. A simple line chart shows net worth (or your top number) over time.

options.label: Keep history
pros: See progress month to month.
Small: years of daily totals fit easily.
cons: The chart starts empty and fills in from the day you start.
Old totals are kept, which matters if this page syncs (see the privacy page).

options.label: Today only
pros: Nothing old is kept.
cons: No sense of progress.

steps.intro: Some accounts connect through Plaid; the rest are typed in. These decide how the numbers stay fresh and how you know when one is old.

steps.path: Opening the page, and its refresh button
steps.headline: When should connected accounts update?
steps.today: Pages update only while open: when you open one, or press its refresh button. Nothing updates while YouCoded is closed.
steps.problem: Plaid gives two kinds of balance: one it checks about once a day (included), and an up-to-the-minute check that costs a small fee every time.
steps.proposal: Pick how the page fetches balances.

options.label: Daily, on open
options.summary: Opening the page shows Plaid's once-a-day balances. A separate "check now" button asks the bank directly.
pros: Free day to day; you only pay for a check you ask for.
Fast to open.
cons: Numbers can be up to a day behind unless you press "check now".

options.label: Live, every open
pros: Always as current as the bank.
cons: A fee every time you open the page, for every account.
Slower to open.

steps.headline: How old can an account's number get before the page warns you?
steps.today: Every account will show when it last updated. Banks sometimes quietly stop sharing until you log in again.
steps.problem: A stale number looks exactly like a fresh one, so you could trust a balance that is a week old.
steps.proposal: Past a cutoff, the account dims and shows "out of date — reconnect" (or "update me" for typed-in accounts).

options.label: 3 days
pros: Catches a broken connection quickly without warning over a weekend.
cons: Typed-in accounts would warn often unless their own cutoff is longer.

options.label: 1 day
pros: Strictest.
cons: Warnings whenever Plaid is a few hours late.

options.label: 7 days
pros: Quiet.
cons: A broken connection can go unnoticed for a week.

steps.path: Accounts that can't connect (likely MOHELA, Earnest, Affirm, Robinhood Gold card, Liberty Mutual, Visible)
steps.headline: How should accounts that can't connect get updated?
steps.today: Some of your accounts will not connect through Plaid. Their numbers have to come from somewhere.
steps.problem: If updating them is a chore, they go stale and the totals stop being true.
steps.proposal: Pick how those numbers get in.

options.label: On the page and by chat
options.summary: An edit button on each account, and you can also tell me ("Earnest is $14,200").
pros: Use whichever is handy.
Chat also lets me fill things in from statement emails later.
cons: Needs the new "I can edit page data" feature (next page).

options.label: On the page only
pros: Works with what Pages can already do.
cons: You have to open the page and type.

options.label: By chat only
pros: No forms on the page.
cons: Can't fix a number without opening a chat.

steps.headline: Should the first version show recent purchases, or balances only?
steps.today: You'd still check each bank's app for individual purchases.
steps.problem: Purchases make the page much bigger: more to design, more data stored and synced, and Plaid charges for it monthly per bank.
steps.proposal: Pick the scope of the first version.

options.label: Balances only
pros: Smaller, faster first version.
Less personal data stored.
cons: Still need the bank app to see what a charge was.

options.label: Recent purchases too
pros: One place for everything.
cons: Larger build, ongoing Plaid cost, and every purchase stored in the page.

steps.intro: This is a feature for every page, not just this one — a grocery list, workout log or reading list would use it the same way.

steps.headline: Which pages should I be allowed to change when you ask me in chat?
steps.today: A page saves its own data. I can build and redesign pages, but I'm told never to change the numbers or lists inside one.
steps.problem: "Add eggs to my grocery page" or "Earnest is $14,200" means you have to open the page and type it yourself.
steps.proposal: The app gives me a safe way to change a page's data: the page describes what its data looks like so I can't save junk, an open page updates instantly, and every change goes into the page's history so it can be undone.

options.label: Pages you allow
options.summary: The first time I try to change a page, you're asked once — the same way pages ask before going online.
pros: A sensitive page stays off-limits unless you say yes.
cons: One extra approval per page.

options.label: Every page
pros: Nothing to approve.
cons: Your money page is editable by me from any chat without you agreeing first.

options.label: None for now
pros: Smaller project.
cons: All typed-in accounts are updated by hand on the page.

steps.path: The chat, right after I change a page
steps.headline: When I change a page's data, how should you find out?
steps.problem: A change you didn't notice — like a mistyped balance — makes the page quietly wrong.
steps.proposal: Pick how my changes show up.

options.label: Note with Undo
options.summary: A small card in chat: "Money page — Earnest $15,100 → $14,200" with an Undo button.
pros: You see every change, and fixing a mistake is one press.
cons: A little more in the chat.

options.label: Ask every time
pros: Nothing changes without a yes.
cons: Slow when I update several accounts at once.

options.label: Just do it
pros: Quietest.
cons: Mistakes are invisible until you notice a wrong number.

steps.headline: Should I be able to read your money page to answer questions like "how much do I owe?"
steps.today: I can't see what's inside a page's saved data during a chat.
steps.problem: Questions like "can I afford this?" or "which card should I pay first?" need me to see your balances.
steps.proposal: Yes: I can read the page when you ask, which sends those numbers to the AI model for that chat (the same as typing them to me). No: I can only change numbers you tell me, never read them. Don't know: we decide after the page exists.

steps.intro: Where your balances are stored, and whose name goes on the Plaid account.

steps.path: Your Personal folder, which syncs between your computers
steps.headline: Should your money page's numbers sync to your other computer?
steps.today: Pages live in your Personal folder, which syncs between your computers and keeps a history of every past version.
steps.problem: Balances synced means a copy of your finances sits wherever Personal syncs to. Bank access itself never syncs; it stays locked in each computer's password storage.

options.label: Sync normally
pros: See the page on both computers.
Connecting a bank on the second computer would use up more of Plaid's 10 free logins — syncing avoids that.
cons: A copy of your balances (and their history) sits in your sync storage.

options.label: This computer only
pros: Your numbers never leave this laptop.
cons: The page is empty on the other computer.
Needs a new "don't sync this page" option built.

steps.path: Plaid's application for real (not practice) bank access
steps.headline: Whose name goes on the Plaid application?
steps.today: Plaid's form asks for "company information". It isn't clear whether it accepts a person instead of a company.
steps.problem: Whoever applies signs Plaid's agreement and is responsible for how the bank data is handled.
steps.proposal: Pick how to apply. This is for your own data only, so the responsibility is about your own accounts.

options.label: You, then LLC
options.summary: Apply as yourself; if Plaid refuses, apply again as your LLC.
pros: Keeps your company out of a personal project if Plaid allows it.
cons: Might cost a day if the first try is refused.

options.label: LLC from the start
pros: Most likely to be approved the first time.
cons: Puts your company's name on a personal-use account.
